notes.label: Label Text
notes.content: In North Africa silver coins were often melted down and made into jewelry, a practice still in use today. In Ethiopia,18th century thaler coins from Austria were preferred. The thaler was popular because it was difficult to "clip" since it had writing on the side of the coin. The combination of a ruler and a crowned double eagle also appealed to local symbolism. While sometimes the coin was used directly as a pendant, more often it was melted down to fashion neck crosses, liturgical crowns and similar adornments.

notes.label: Label Text
notes.content: This is an important Ethiopian Orthodox icon that was once owned by a parsonage. On the proper right panel it depicts the gruesome scene of St. George being chopped into pieces below the twelve apostles and the saint himself killing a dragon. The proper left panel features the Virgin Mary and child with an angel above each shoulder.

notes.label: Label Text
notes.content: It has been suggested that this diptych is strongly influenced by, or directly copied from, a triptych by Nicolo Brancaleon, an Italian Renaissance painter. However, the chopping tool used here is particularly Ethiopian, as is the depiction of the Virgin and Child, lacking among known Brancaleon works.

notes.label: Label Text
notes.content: Ethiopian paintings influenced by European art are, according to Stanislaw Chojnacki, of two kinds: paintings that directly relate to an identified painting, and paintings which borrow themes and details from Western art. In both, however, the Western forms have been simplified to the Ethiopian mode of expression. This diptych is of the first example, which, though more rare, illustrates the impact of the expatriate European artist. Ethiopian artists-in-training preferred to copy paintings, and perhaps this diptych came from a European workshop in Ethiopia, made directly from an existing painting by Nicolo Brancaleon, as suggested by Chojnacki.

notes.label: Label Text
notes.content: Chojnacki, Stanislaw. 1983. Major Themes in Ethiopian Painting: Indigenous Developments, The Influence of Foreign Models and their Adaptation from the 13th to the 19th Century. Wiesbaden: Steiner (Series: Äthiopistische Forschungen; -- Bd. 10), pp. 418-419.
